intro: St Peter Port is the harbour town of Guernsey, climbing steeply from the quays to the open green of Cambridge Park on its northern edge. On the park's lawn stands a hollow old sweet chestnut whose broken heart is ringed by living limbs that sweep low over the grass. A reader photographed it in late autumn and sent it to us, as an oak of 400 years by their estimate.

trees.story:
A reader sent us this tree from Cambridge Park, the open green on the edge of St Peter Port in Guernsey, and called it an oak of 400 years.

Look at the leaves still hanging in its crown and lying on the grass, though, and they are long, narrow and saw-edged, the leaves of a sweet chestnut. Tell us if you know it better. Whatever its name, it is a veteran. The central trunk has burst open and gone hollow, a tall broken column of pale, weathered wood swollen with burrs, and around it the tree has rebuilt itself. Thick grey limbs swing out low over the grass in every direction and then climb again into a wide crown, the way an old chestnut keeps on living long after its heart has rotted away. A sawn log lies on the lawn nearby, and a monkey puzzle stands among the shrubs behind.

The 400 years are the reader's estimate; we have no girth, planting date or record for the tree yet. If you know it, or what the parish says about it, tell us here and we will add it with your figures.

Go in late autumn, as the reader did, when the last copper leaves hang in the crown, and walk all the way round the hollow trunk.
trees.how_to_recognise: On the open lawn: a burst, hollow column of pale dead wood at the centre, ringed by thick grey living limbs that sweep low over the grass and then climb, a monkey puzzle among the shrubs behind.

question_context: A reader who walked across Cambridge Park, the open green on the northern edge of St Peter Port, sent us a photograph of this tree in late autumn and called it an oak of about 400 years. The leaves still hanging in its crown and lying on the grass are long, narrow and saw-edged, which are the leaves of a sweet chestnut, so that is how we list it, and we ask readers to tell us if they know better. It is plainly a veteran. The central trunk has burst open and gone hollow, a tall broken column of pale weathered wood swollen with burrs, and around it thick grey living limbs swing out low over the lawn and climb again into a wide crown. That is how old chestnuts carry on for centuries after their heartwood rots. The age is the reader's estimate; we have no girth, planting date or written record for the tree yet. The park is public and free to walk in, and the tree stands on its open grass with a monkey puzzle among the shrubs behind it.

faq.q: Can I visit The Hollow Chestnut of Cambridge Park?
faq.a: Yes. It stands on the open lawn of Cambridge Park, a public park on the edge of St Peter Port, free to enter.

faq.q: How old is the chestnut in Cambridge Park?
faq.a: The reader who sent it puts it at about 400 years. We have no measurement or record yet; if you know one, tell us on its page.

faq.q: Is it an oak or a chestnut?
faq.a: The reader sent it as an oak, but the long, saw-edged leaves in its crown and on the grass are a sweet chestnut's.
